title: Novel Scoring System for Prediction of Cardiac Syndrome X in Women with Typical Angina and a Positive Exercise Tolerance Test
abstract: A major diagnostic challenge for cardiologists is to distinguish cardiac syndrome X (CSX) from obstructive coronary artery disease in women with typical angina and a positive exercise tolerance test (ETT). We performed this study to develop a scoring system that more accurately predicts CSX in this patient population. Data on 976 women with typical angina and a positive ETT who underwent coronary angiography at our center were randomly divided into derivation and validation datasets. We developed a backward stepwise logistic regression model that predicted the presence of CSX, and a scoring system was derived from it. The derivation dataset (809 patients) was calibrated by uing a Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (8 degrees of freedom; χ2=12.9; P=0.115), and the area under the curve was 0.758. The validation dataset (167 patients) was calibrated in the same way (8 degrees of freedom; χ2=9.0; P=0.339), and the area under the curve was 0.782. Independent predictors of CSX were age <55 years; negative histories of smoking, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, or familial premature coronary artery disease; and highly positive ETTs. A total score >9.5 was the optimal cutoff point for differentiating CSX from obstructive coronary artery disease. Our proposed scoring system is a simple, objective, and accurate system for distinguishing CSX from obstructive coronary artery disease in women with typical angina and positive ETTs. It may help determine which of these patients need invasive coronary angiograms or noninvasive tests like computed tomographic coronary angiography.

title: PCV104 Real World Evidence Versus Quality of Test Study Results in Diagnostics for Coronary Heart Disease
Prediction and Analysis of Heart Disease Using Machine Learning
abstract: Heart disease is one of the most significant causes of global mortality since its intricacy and the rate of misdiagnosis have brought a great challenge to medical workers. As machine learning has shown robust efficacy in decision-making and predictions, it is essential to construct a machine learning model to assist with heart disease diagnosis. In this paper, a heart-disease dataset from Cleveland was analyzed and preprocessed including cleaning, one-hot encoding, and standardization, and preliminary findings of relevant features to heart disease were discovered, such as male. In the process of model training, six machine learning algorithms (Logistic Regression, K-nearest Neighbors, Adaboost, CART, Random Forest, XGBoost) were applied, and the Random Forest was determined to be the optimal model after hyperparameter tuning and cross-validation as it outperformed other models with superior scores of accuracy (0.848), f1 (0.829), PRC-AUC (0.909), and ROC-AUC (0.917). In addition, the most relevant features, including reversible defect of thallium stress test, high ST depression caused by exercise relative to rest, and asymptomatic chest pain, etc., were unearthed by plotting permutation feature importance and partial importance plots of the Random Forest classifier.
venue: International Conference on Robotics, Automation and Artificial Intelligence (RAAI)

title: Comparing American and European Guidelines for the Initial Diagnosis of Stable Ischaemic Heart Disease
abstract: Ischaemic heart disease (IHD) is common, with a global prevalence of 110.55 million cases in 2015, and remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide.1 Non-invasive cardiac testing accounts for a substantial portion of healthcare spending in the USA, representing more than 40% of Medicare Part B expenditures on medical imaging (over $17 billion annually) in a recent analysis.2 Inappropriate cardiac stress testing is responsible for over $500 million in healthcare costs yearly in the USA.3 While professional societies have developed appropriate use criteria (AUC) to guide selection of stress testing for patients with suspected stable ischaemic heart disease (SIHD), adherence to them is suboptimal.4,5 A systematic review in 2015 found that 48% of stress echocardiograms and 32% of single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) scans were considered inappropriate according to AUC.5 Fewer than half of patients with a positive non-invasive stress test referred for invasive coronary angiography (ICA) are found to have angiographic evidence of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD).6 In the face of rising healthcare costs and a transition to reimbursement models based on value and clinical outcomes, there is an urgent need to consider the diagnostic accuracy and cost-effectiveness of different stress testing modalities and target non-invasive assessment to patients who are most likely to benefit. The new European Society of Cardiology (ESC) chronic coronary syndromes (CCS) guideline, released in August 2019, includes a comprehensive series of recommendations on diagnosis, risk assessment, and management of this insidious disease.7 While the 2013 ESC guidelines referred to stable CAD, a shift in terminology to CCS is used to emphasize its chronic and progressive nature. American guidelines on SIHD, last published in 2012, as a collaboration among the American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA) Task Force on Practice Guidelines, American College of Physicians, American Association for Thoracic Surgery, Preventive Cardiovascular Nurses Association, Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions, and Society of Thoracic Surgeons, include recommendations on the full spectrum of care in CCS/SIHD.8 In this review, we will focus on the initial diagnosis of CCS/SIHD and describe how the ESC guidelines encourage a transition from exercise electrocardiogram (ECG) testing to universal imaging-based assessment. A primary goal of stress testing is to identify the presence or absence of obstructive CAD for patients without established IHD. Functional tests aim to identify myocardial ischaemia and are inferred to represent obstructive CAD. Common functional modalities include exercise ECG, stress echocardiography, perfusion imaging with SPECT or positron emission tomography (PET), and stress cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Anatomic tests enable direct visualization of coronary artery stenoses, but do not provide definitive evidence of haemodynamic significance unless supplemented with non-invasive or invasive assessment of fractional flow reserve (FFR) or coronary flow reserve. Anatomic imaging modalities used in clinical practice include computed tomography angiography (CTA), ICA, and cardiac magnetic resonance angiography, each with different test characteristics and limitations. Despite limited sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of SIHD, initial exercise ECG testing was thought to be more cost-effective than imaging-based assessment in most cases and has been a preferred test since the 1960s. However, studies in the UK have demonstrated that exercise echocardiography is more cost-effective compared to exercise ECG alone.9,10 Similarly, SPECT improves risk prediction after exercise ECG in a cost-effective fashion.11 In terms of anatomic imaging, coronary CTA has emerged as a likely cost-effective initial diagnostic test for patients with low to intermediate pre-test probability (PTP) of obstructive CAD.12 In the USA, insurance companies [through radiology benefit management (RBM) programs] often restrict providers from using imaging-based stress testing to reduce costs and use proprietary algorithms for approval of tests that do not always align with AUC published by the ACC or AHA.13,14 Contemporary studies that evaluate cost-effectiveness of exercise ECG vs. initial imaging-based screening will be mandatory before insurers and their RBMs are likely to change their current protocols. Until recently, American and European guidelines both recommended exercise ECG as the initial stress test for most patients with suspected IHD, particularly those with an interpretable baseline ECG, who have an intermediate PTP of IHD and are able to exercise. The 2019 ESC CCS guidelines now recommend non-invasive functional imaging such as stress echocardiography, PET, SPECT, or anatomic assessment with coronary CTA as the initial diagnostic test for suspected IHD in cases where clinical assessment alone is insufficient to exclude obstructive CAD.7 The guidelines suggest that exercise ECG may be used as an alternative when imaging is not available, or as a complementary test to assess exercise tolerance, symptoms and event risk. Key differences in stress testing recommendations between the ESC and ACC/AHA guidelines are summarized in Table 1. Initial stress testing recommendations for patients with suspected stable ischemic heart disease/chronic coronary syndrome who are able to exercise: Key guideline statements at a glance Initial stress testing recommendations for patients with suspected stable ischemic heart disease/chronic coronary syndrome who are able to exercise: Key guideline statements at a glance The evaluation of a patient with suspected SIHD begins with a targeted history, physical examination, and resting ECG. The patient’s age, sex, and chest pain characteristics can be used to estimate the PTP of obstructive CAD. Both guidelines agree that non-invasive testing is most useful for patients with an intermediate PTP. The precise definition of intermediate PTP is arbitrary: American guidelines note that a range of 10–90% is reasonable, while European guidelines use >15% (no upper limit specified, although 65% has been used historically). American guidelines offer two tables for estimating PTP, one based on combined Diamond/Forrester and Coronary Artery Surgery Study data and the other based on the Duke Databank for Cardiovascular Disease, which provides estimates for low- and high-risk patients based on the presence or absence of diabetes mellitus, smoking, and hyperlipidaemia. The ACC/AHA guideline points out that both datasets may overestimate IHD likelihood in lower-risk patients and women and suggests that testing should be deferred for patients with a PTP of <5% due to high likelihood of a false-positive test. Based on these risk stratification tools, only a minority of patients (low-risk men in their 30 s with non-anginal pain, low-risk women < age 55 with non-anginal pain, and low-risk women in their 30 s with atypical angina) can be ruled out for obstructive CAD on clinical criteria alone (Table 2). Pretest probability estimatesa of obstructive CAD from 2012 ACC/AHA guideline. Pretest probability estimatesa of obstructive CAD from 2012 ACC/AHA guideline. In contrast, the new ESC guidelines provide an updated PTP algorithm based on a pooled analysis of contemporary cohorts with significantly lower PTP estimates across the spectrum of age, sex, and chest pain characteristics (Table 3). Pre-test probability estimates for elderly patients (age 70+) are included in the ESC guideline but not in the ACC/AHA recommendations. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors and previously performed non-invasive testing can be used to refine the clinical likelihood of CAD. The European authors specify that non-invasive testing should be deferred for patients with PTP ≤5%, while testing can be considered for some patients with PTP of 5–15%. If non-invasive testing is restricted to patients with at least intermediate PTP (>15%), obstructive CAD can be excluded on clinical grounds in many subgroups (including men and women in their 30 s with typical angina, men and women in their 40 s with atypical angina, and men and women in their 50 s with non-anginal chest pain) who are often referred for testing. In an analysis of the Prospective Multicenter Imaging Study for Evaluation of Chest Pain (PROMISE) trial, half of patients initially classified as intermediate PTP for obstructive CAD were reclassified as low risk (<15%) using contemporary PTP estimates.7,15 Targeting non-invasive testing to patients who are at least intermediate risk based on contemporary PTP estimates has the potential to reduce false-positive results, improve the diagnostic yield of ICA, identify patients who are most likely to benefit from preventative therapies, and reduce costs. Pretest probability estimates of obstructive CAD from 2019 ESC CCS guideline. Pretest probability estimates of obstructive CAD from 2019 ESC CCS guideline. The ideal stress test should have adequate diagnostic power to reclassify a patient’s level of risk for major adverse cardiovascular events, provide prognostic information to help guide subsequent management decisions, and be cost-effective. As noted above, a key difference between the American and European guidelines is downgrading of exercise ECG to a second-line stress testing modality in the ESC recommendations. The European authors emphasize the inferior diagnostic power of exercise ECG, citing evidence that it can rule out significant CAD only when PTP is ≤19% and rule in CAD when PTP is ≥80%.16 Functional imaging modalities (including SPECT, PET, and stress CMR) were superior, with the ability to rule out functionally significant CAD at PTPs ranging from ≤34% to 57% and rule in significant CAD at PTPs ranging from ≥46% to 59%. Coronary CTA demonstrated a similar negative predictive value but a lower positive predictive value for functionally significant CAD, with rule-out and rule-in PTP ranges of ≤57% and ≥75%, respectively.16 Despite their recommendation for upfront ECG exercise testing for most patients, the American authors acknowledge that imaging, particularly nuclear myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) such as SPECT or PET and stress echocardiography, can provide additional prognostic value over exercise ECG alone and may improve event prediction even for patients with low-risk Duke treadmill scores.17,18 In a recent network meta-analysis of non-invasive testing for patients with CCS and low-risk acute coronary syndromes, exercise ECG generated the highest rate of follow-up testing.19 In the context of contemporary PTP estimates that are much lower than historical data, there is a strong rationale for initial selection of an imaging-based stress test to avoid false-positive results and unnecessary additional testing. Two key trials of coronary CTA, the Scottish Computed Tomography of the Heart Trial (SCOT-HEART) and PROMISE, have been published since the release of the American SIHD guidelines and inform recommendations for the 2019 European guidelines.20–22 SCOT-HEART included outpatients with a mean age of 57.1 years (56% male) presenting with stable chest pain, most of whom had normal exercise ECG testing before randomization to standard care vs. standard care plus coronary CTA. Remarkably, the primary endpoint of death from CAD and non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI) occurred less frequently in the coronary CTA group compared to standard care alone [2.3% vs. 3.9%; hazard ratio (HR) 0.59; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.41–0.84; P = 0.04], with similar overall rates of coronary angiography and revascularization in each group over a median follow-up of 4.8 years. PROMISE enrolled a similar population and compared a primary composite outcome of mortality, MI, hospitalization for unstable angina, or major procedural complication for patients randomized to initial coronary CTA or functional testing (most commonly MPI). Initial coronary CTA compared to functional testing did not reduce the primary composite outcome over a median follow-up of 25 months (3.3% vs. 3.0%; adjusted HR 1.04, 95% CI 0.83–1.29; P = 0.75). A subsequent analysis of the PROMISE data demonstrated that coronary CTA provided better discriminatory ability to predict adverse events compared to functional imaging (c-index, 0.72; 95% CI 0.68–0.76 vs. 0.64, 95% CI 0.59–0.69; P = 0.04), likely by identifying patients at risk for events because of the presence of non-obstructive CAD.22 The discrepancy in topline results between SCOT-HEART and PROMISE may be related to shorter follow-up and less emphasis on starting preventative therapies for non-obstructive CAD which accounted for the majority of subsequent adverse cardiac events in the PROMISE CTA group.22 Patients enrolled in the CTA arm of SCOT-HEART were more likely to start treatment with aspirin and statin therapy compared to the standard of care group (odds ratio 1.40, 95% CI 1.19–1.65) and may explain the improved outcomes associated with CTA.20,23 Coronary CTA-derived FFR may enhance the diagnostic and prognostic utility of CTA, but this technique is highly dependent upon adequate image quality and is not well-validated in intermediate-risk patient populations nor widely available in clinical practice.24–26 American guidelines state that coronary CTA might be reasonable as a first-line test for patients with intermediate PTP of IHD who are unable to exercise or have contraindications to stress testing. Citing evidence from the recent coronary CTA trials, European guidelines go a step further and assign a Class I recommendation to coronary CTA as an initial test for patients with low clinical likelihood of CAD. The high negative predictive value of coronary CTA makes it particularly valuable in ruling out CAD in low-risk populations. Both guidelines agree that it can be used to clarify an equivocal result from functional testing. Importantly, it should be avoided if there are factors associated with poor image quality (such as significant obesity, dense coronary calcification, and inability to cooperate with directions during the scan).7 In the International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness With Medical and Invasive Approaches (ISCHEMIA) trial presented at 2019 AHA Scientific Sessions, investigators used coronary CTA to define coronary anatomy for patients with at least moderate ischaemia on a functional stress test before randomization to an initial strategy of conservative or invasive management. Patients with unprotected left main disease or non-obstructive CAD on coronary CTA were not randomized. Over a median follow-up of 3.3 years, an initial strategy of revascularization compared to conservative guideline-directed medical therapy did not reduce the primary outcome of cardiovascular death, MI, hospitalization for unstable angina, heart failure, or resuscitated cardiac arrest (adjusted HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.80–1.08; P = 0.34).27 Notably, lack of obstructive CAD (present in 14% of screened patients) on coronary CTA was one of the major reasons that screened patients were not randomized in the trial. The use of coronary CTA for risk stratification in SIHD patients will likely increase in light of the results from the ISCHEMIA trial. For patients with high PTP of CAD, ICA is a reasonable initial test. While the American authors do not make a formal recommendation about ICA in this setting, they cite evidence that it is not cost-effective for patients with PTP of CAD <75–80%.28,29 Over the past decade, evidence has emerged that use of invasive haemodynamic assessment with FFR or instantaneous wave-free ratio improves clinical outcomes over angiography alone when used to guide percutaneous coronary intervention.30–32 The European guidelines recommend ICA as an alternative initial test for CAD diagnosis for patients with high clinical likelihood and severe symptoms, noting that invasive haemodynamic assessment should be used to assess angiographic stenoses <90% before revascularization. Although the contemporary practice of diagnostic left heart catheterization is very safe, it is worth noting that potential complications such as death, MI, stroke, coronary dissection, cardiac tamponade, and need for urgent bypass surgery, can be avoided with an approach that utilizes non-invasive imaging as a first-line modality, even for high PTP patients.33 The recently published 2019 ESC CCS guidelines represent a major departure from initial screening for IHD with exercise ECG to imaging-based protocols. When used to evaluate patients with suspected SIHD, non-invasive functional and anatomic imaging tests outperform exercise ECG and may be more cost-effective. Coronary CTA has been shown to improve outcomes by targeting preventative therapies for patients with low to intermediate PTP of IHD who are found to have non-obstructive CAD. Contemporary PTP estimates of CAD should be used to guide selection of diagnostic testing. Coronary CTA is most helpful for scenarios of low PTP, while non-invasive functional imaging is preferred for settings of intermediate to high PTP and initial ICA with haemodynamic assessment is reasonable for patients with high PTP. While exercise ECG still has a role for assessing functional capacity, symptom burden, and prognosis, initial non-invasive imaging should be strongly considered to clarify both CAD diagnosis and prognosis. The next iteration of the American guidelines will likely reflect contemporary studies of imaging-based risk assessment and PTP, although implementation of new recommendations may be constrained by opposition from payers and value-based care delivery models that may balk at the increased upfront costs of non-invasive imaging protocols. Future studies will need to show the cost-effectiveness of non-invasive imaging over exercise ECG testing and demonstrate the benefits of targeted preventative therapies based on identification of non-obstructive CAD in prospective randomized trials. title: Healthcare with emphasis on coronary thrombosis prediction
abstract: Heart attacks, also known as cardiac arrests, have become a leading cause of death globally in recent decades. They represent the culmination of intricate relationships between modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Many cases of cardiovascular disease can be attributed to factors that can be changed, making prevention possible for most cases. This research aims to develop a predictive model for the likelihood of patients experiencing a heart attack using pre-existing datasets from the UCI Heart repository database. In the study, classifiers were employed in a pipeline approach to machine learning, performing predictions in both directions, with and without optimizations and feature transformations. The findings indicate that the Random Forest classifier achieved the highest accuracy score in binary prediction, where 1 signifies a possibility of a heart attack and 0 denotes no chance. Factors such as age, cholesterol level (with levels above 200 mg/dl being more susceptible), increased heart rate, and the type of chest pain (with typical angina being the most common and asymptomatic chest pain being the least) were found to have the most significant influence on the prediction model.

title: Comparative and Explainable Machine Learning for Coronary Artery Disease Classification
abstract: Accurate and interpretable classification of angiographically defined coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a relevant benchmark for clinical machine-learning research. This study compares eight supervised-learning models using the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. After complete-case exclusion, 297 records with 13 clinical and diagnostic predictors were analyzed. Nominal predictors were one-hot encoded, binary predictors were retained in their original coding, and continuous predictors were standardized for scale-sensitive models. Preprocessing parameters were estimated using training data only and re-estimated within each cross-validation fold. Logistic Regression, a Decision Tree, k-Nearest Neighbors, a Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, a Support Vector Machine, and an equal-weight Soft-Voting Ensemble were assessed using a stratified 80/20 train–test split and stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Test performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, confusion matrices, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Under stratified 10-fold cross-validation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest mean accuracy (83.83%), followed by the Multilayer Perceptron (83.16%), while Logistic Regression also achieved the highest mean ROC AUC (0.9093). On the complementary 60-record held-out test partition, the Support Vector Machine and Multilayer Perceptron achieved the highest observed accuracy (86.67%), whereas the Support Vector Machine achieved the highest ROC AUC (0.9565). Tree-based feature-importance analyses and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis of the Gradient-Boosting model showed relatively large model-attribution values for the number of major vessels visualized by fluoroscopy, the asymptomatic chest-pain category, age, ST-segment depression, cholesterol, and specific thallium stress-test categories. More complex models showed no consistent performance advantage. Excluding the fluoroscopy-derived predictor ca reduced mean cross-validation accuracy and ROC AUC for all eight classifiers. In the more restrictive seven-predictor analysis, which additionally excluded thallium and exercise-test variables, the highest mean cross-validation accuracy was 78.15% (Logistic Regression), while the highest ROC AUC was 0.8315 (Random Forest). Given the small, historical, single-center sample, the inclusion of target-proximal diagnostic predictors, the absence of calibration assessment, and the lack of external validation, the findings should be interpreted as an internal comparative benchmark rather than evidence of clinical applicability or readiness for clinical deployment.

title: Stress-only myocardial perfusion scintigraphy: a prospective study on the accuracy and observer agreement with quantitative coronary angiography as the gold standard
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Patients with normal stress perfusion have an excellent prognosis. Prospective studies on the diagnostic accuracy of stress-only scans with contemporary, independent examinations as gold standards are lacking. PATIENTS AND METHODS: A total of 109 patients with typical angina and no previous coronary artery disease underwent a 2-day stress (exercise)/rest, gated, and attenuation-corrected (AC), 99m-technetium-sestamibi perfusion study, followed by invasive coronary angiography. The stress datasets were evaluated twice by four physicians with two different training levels (expert and novice): familiar and unfamiliar with AC. The two experts also made a consensus reading of the integrated stress-rest datasets. The consensus reading and quantitative data from the invasive coronary angiography were applied as reference methods. RESULTS: The sensitivity/specificity were 0.92-1.00/0.73-0.90 (reference: expert consensus reading), 0.93-0.96/0.63-0.82 (reference: ≥1 stenosis>70%), and 0.75-0.88/0.70-0.88 (reference: ≥1 stenosis>50%). The four readers showed a high and fairly equal sensitivity independent of their familiarity with AC. The expert familiar with AC had the highest specificity independent of the reference method. The intraobserver and interobserver agreements on the stress-only readings were good (readers without AC experience) to excellent (readers with AC experience). CONCLUSION: AC stress-only images yielded a high sensitivity independent of the training level and experience with AC of the nuclear physician, whereas the specificity correlated positively with both. Interobserver and intraobserver agreements tended to be the best for physicians with AC experience.

title: ANALISIS PENGARUH JENIS NYERI DADA TERHADAP RATA-RATA TEKANAN DARAH DAN USIA MENGGUNAKAN MANOVA
abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of chest pain type on mean blood pressure and age using the Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) method. Chest pain is a common symptom that can indicate various health conditions, including heart disease. The data used in this study was taken from the "Heart Failure Prediction ” dataset downloaded from Kaggle, which included variables such as chest pain type, blood pressure, and patient age. MANOVA analysis was performed to test whether there were significant differences in blood pressure and age based on the type of chest pain (Typical Angina, Atypical Angina, Non-Anginal Pain, and Asymptomatic). MANOVA test results showed that at least one type of chest pain significantly affected blood pressure and age. Multiple comparison tests were conducted to identify differences between chest pain groups. This study concluded that chest pain type significantly affected blood pressure, but no significant difference was found in age based on chest pain type. These findings may help in the diagnosis and management of patients with chest pain, and provide important information for the prevention of cardiovascular complications.

title: Transparent AI in Healthcare: Achieving Dual-Level Interpretability Using Shapley Values
abstract: The integration of machine learning in cardiology offers immense diagnostic potential, yet the "black box" nature of advanced algorithms hinders clinical adoption. Medical professionals require predictive tools that are both highly accurate and strictly interpretable. Clinicians must trust a model’s underlying medical reasoning across diverse populations, while also possessing the ability to explain individual risk assessments to patients. In this project, we developed an XGBoost model using a multi-hospital heart disease dataset and applied SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to achieve full-spectrum clinical transparency. Globally, SHAP feature importance proved the model consistently anchored predictions on biologically sound, universal risk factors—such as asymptomatic chest pain and oldpeak—across entirely different healthcare systems. Locally, SHAP waterfall plots deconstructed individual predictions, translating complex mathematical log-odds into clear, feature-by-feature patient risk profiles. Our findings demonstrate that advanced models need not sacrifice explainability for accuracy. By bridging complex mathematics and actionable clinical insights through dual-level SHAP interpretability, this approach ensures AI can be confidently and safely deployed in real-world healthcare settings.

title: HD-SMART: A Novel Machine Learning Framework for High-Accuracy Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Using Advanced Feature Engineering
abstract: This work presents a novel concept known as Heart Disease Systematic Machine learning Analytical Risk prediction Technology (HD-SMART) that is considered a unique perspective in handling cardiac disease and the identification of sophisticated risk markers using superior computational technology. The work offers a rather peculiar approach to harnessing multiple machine learning algorithms in combination with feature selection methods that proved themselves highly accurate in cardiovascular risk estimation. The novelty is that these algorithms, namely, the Random Forest, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Logistic Regression, are to be adopted in a systematic manner with supplementary feature engineering and with hyperparameter optimization, respectively. Based on the UCI Heart Disease dataset of 303 instances with 14 attributes, the new HD-SMART framework illustrated exceptional predictive capability, with the Random Forest at 97.57%, followed by SVM (95.23%) and Logistic Regression at 94.18%. The methodology achieved unique convergent optimization regarding feature selection with a minimum cost function of 0.0004 at iteration 50, while the Root Mean Square Error convergence was reached within the first four iterations with a value of 0.030. The innovative approach of data preprocessing and feature analysis in the framework pointed out critical patterns in cardiological parameters, such as in chest pain distribution (n ≈ 410 typical angina cases), bimodal blood pressure peaks (130–140 mmHg and 190–200 mmHg), as well as electrocardiogram variabilities (450 normal and 350 ST-T-wave abnormalities). The new proportion of 70–30 train-test split ratio was more optimal for model performance. This work introduces a completely new, computational diagnostic approach that not only outperforms but significantly surpasses conventional methods, and its robust statistical validity is maintained across a number of performance metrics. HD-SMART contributes to the advancement of cardiovascular diagnosis as a new, effective tool for early detection of heart disease for health practitioners based on big data analysis. title: Convenient timing by “accident” – Resting ischemia detected by resting myocardial perfusion imaging
